overview: Memeware 7.3's Anti Bot is a two-list filter that runs from a single UpdateEvent consumer and feeds a shared combat blacklist. Every tick it walks the loaded entity list, adds any EntityPlayer whose health attribute holds a real number to a private bad list and to the public static CombatUtil.botList, and removes players from botList as soon as their client-side onGround flag is true. The module registers ViperMC, Hypixel and Mineplex server presets, but the handler never reads the selected mode; the same health-and-ground rule runs for all three. Because CombatUtil.getTarget, getTargets and canBlock all skip entities in botList, the filter directly shapes what the Kill Aura module can attack and block against.

sections.p: The module is one Consumer<UpdateEvent> field named fard, annotated with LWJEB's @Handler, plus two static lists. bad is private to the module and accumulates every player that ever passes the health test; CombatUtil.botList is the shared public static list that the combat utilities consult, and every add to bad is mirrored into it. onEnable and onDisable both clear the two lists, so toggling the module rebuilds the filter from scratch. The addModes call registers the ViperMC, Hypixel and Mineplex presets, but the handler body has no switch on the mode setting; the preset selection is cosmetic and every mode executes the identical health-and-ground logic.

The filter's first rule is inverted relative to most bot filters: a player enters bad and botList when Float.isNaN(entityPlayer.getHealth()) is false, meaning the health attribute holds a real number. Entities whose data watcher never supplied health, which is the classic signature of server-side bots, read as Float.NaN and are never flagged. The second rule unflags: whenever entityPlayer.onGround is true and the player is in botList, the module removes it, so a grounded player is presumed real. The combined effect is that the blacklist holds players that are airborne at the moment of the tick, and the killaura stops attacking anything that is not on the ground, including falling players, flying players and hovering NPCs. The onGround value is the client's own simulated flag, so the filter trusts the target's reported ground state rather than checking the world.

CombatUtil.getTarget iterates mc.theWorld.loadedEntityList and returns the first EntityLivingBase within range that is alive, not invisible (unless allowed), not the local player and not contained in botList. getTargets applies the same skip for the multi-target path, and canBlock returns false when every candidate is in botList, which also disables the blockhit re-block. Because targeting is first-match-in-list with no sorting, filtering only removes candidates; it never reorders what remains. The UpdateEvent handler runs every tick, so a bot that lands is un-flagged and becomes attackable again, and a player that jumps becomes blacklisted for the duration of the jump.

files.label: AntiBot.java (health and ground filter)
files.explanation:
The entire module. The fard consumer is registered with @Handler on UpdateEvent, so it runs once per client tick and walks mc.theWorld.loadedEntityList, casting every EntityPlayer and applying the two rules: a non-NaN health value adds to bad and CombatUtil.botList, and a true onGround flag removes from botList. The class exposes the static bad list that the module itself maintains, while the actionable list lives in CombatUtil so the combat utilities can read it without importing the module.

The mode presets are registered but never consulted: addModes populates the mode setting with ViperMC, Hypixel and Mineplex, and the consumer ignores the setting entirely. onEnable and onDisable both clear bad and CombatUtil.botList, which means a toggle resets the blacklist and the first tick after enable re-evaluates every loaded player. The module never touches a packet class; its only output is the shared list state.

files.label: CombatUtil.java (shared bot blacklist)
files.explanation:
CombatUtil owns the public static botList that AntiBot fills, and every targeting helper consults it. getTarget, getTargets and canBlock each short-circuit on botList.contains(o), so a flagged entity is invisible to the Single and Multi aura paths and never counts as a block target. The list is a raw ArrayList shared across modules with no synchronization, and the AntiBot module both adds and removes entries while the killaura reads it in the same tick.

getTargets also rejects entities that are not EntityPlayer after the botList test, and applies a range bonus of 2 blocks for targets standing above the player. The botList check sits before the entity-type filter, so a flagged player is rejected before any range or type logic runs. This file is what connects the AntiBot module to combat: without it the filter would have no effect on what the aura attacks.

countering.label: Hawk FightHitbox (server-side hit validation)
countering.explanation:
FightHitbox re-validates every player-versus-player attack on the server instead of trusting the client hit-scan. When an InteractEntityEvent arrives, Hawk stores it and waits for the next move packet, because in 1.8 the client computes the attack direction from the yaw and pitch of the frame, and the movement packet that carries them arrives after the use-entity packet. On the move it builds a ray from the attacker's eye position (y plus 1.62, minus 0.08 while sneaking) along that direction, expands the victim's hitbox by a 0.005 epsilon, and requires the ray to intersect the box within MAX_REACH, 3.1 blocks in survival and 5.0 in creative.

The victim position is rewound through the lag compensator to the ping-appropriate history location, so the box is checked where the attacker actually saw it. When the ray misses the box entirely and CHECK_BOX_INTERSECTION is on, Hawk punishes with 'Did not hit hitbox.'; when it intersects but the distance exceeds the reach, the violation reports the measured reach in meters. The optional CHECK_OCCLUSION path also walks a block iterator from the eye along the ray and flags any hit whose intersection with a solid block is closer than the victim, which catches through-wall attacks.

The Memeware killaura attacks without any line-of-sight test and aims from a fixed eye height of posY plus 1.2 at ent.posY plus half the eye height, with the yaw and pitch snapped into the UpdateEvent on the same tick the C02 is sent. The server-visible direction therefore points at the target's upper body, and the geometry must intersect the lag-compensated box within 3.1 blocks. An attack from the module's default 6-block range at a target standing further than 3.1 from the eye fails the distance test, and an attack aimed through a wall trips the occlusion path when enabled. The client-side bot filter does not matter to this check: it validates every C02 geometrically regardless of which entities the client decided to attack.

countering.label: Arc KillAura (direction, reach and speed)
countering.explanation:
Arc's KillAura check runs five sub-checks over each attack. Direction computes the angle between the player's look vector and the vector to the attacked entity and flags when it exceeds max-direction-angle. Multi compares the angle to the previously attacked entity when the target switched and both entities are within reach, catching multi-target auras. NoSwing flags when the time since the last arm swing exceeds max-swing-time, Reach measures the distance to the entity minus its velocity against max-reach, and Speed counts total attacks and attack packets per second against max-attacks and max-attack-packets.

The Memeware aura sends swingItem() before every C02, so NoSwing passes as long as the swing packet is not dropped. The attack cadence, however, is a fixed timer at 1000 divided by the click speed, 12 to 20 attacks per second, which is exactly the regime the Speed sub-check is built for: sustained attacks above max-attacks in a one-second window accumulate violations, and the blockhit cycle adds C07 release and C08 re-block packets around each C02, inflating the packet counter that checkFrequency scores.

The reach side is worse for the module: the range setting defaults to 6 and can be raised to 8, while max-reach is a typical combat distance near 3, and the check subtracts only the target's velocity. An attack at 4 or more blocks from the target is a direct violation, and the snap-aimed pitch makes the Direction angle small and constant, which is the one part of the check the module satisfies. The bot filter in CombatUtil.botList changes none of this: it only removes candidates client-side, and every attack that does get sent is scored the same way.

countering.label: NCP Fight Reach (eye-to-box distance)
countering.explanation:
NCP's fight Reach measures the distance from the attacker's eye location to the damaged entity's box, not to its center. The eye position is pLoc.getY() plus the player's eye height, the reference y is clamped into the victim's height range, and with reachPrecision the horizontal distance is reduced by getinset, which projects the player's direction onto the box edge so a player attacking from the side of a wide box gets credit for the box width. The limit is 6.0 in creative and cc.reachSurvivalDistance in survival, plus a per-entity modifier for EnderDragon and Giant.

Violations accumulate reachVL and execute reachActions, and when cancel is true the attack penalty applies. The check also adapts: reachReduce shrinks data.reachMod toward distanceMin whenever hits stay near the limit, so sustained borderline reach tightens the effective envelope, and the Improbable combined check feeds on the violation magnitude. The attack penalty gates further hits for a configured duration, which punishes an aura that keeps attacking at the edge.

The Memeware aura's default range of 6, with an extra 2 blocks for targets standing above the player, sits well beyond the survival limit of about 3.0. Every C02 sent at a target more than the limit away adds its excess distance to reachVL, and the dynamic reachMod means the module cannot simply hover at the limit. The bot filter removes candidates but never changes the geometry of the hits that are sent, so filtered and unfiltered attacks are measured identically.

countering.label: Grim Reach (reconstructed hitbox intercept)
countering.explanation:
Grim's Reach check validates each attack against a server-reconstructed version of the target's hitbox. checkReach builds the possible look directions from the current yaw and pitch plus the last tick's yaw and pitch, extends the eye position along each direction to maxReach plus 3 blocks, and requires ReachUtils.calculateIntercept to find an intersection with the target box; the minimum distance to the box comes from ReachUtils.getMinReachToBox and the violation threshold is 0.0005. When the attack cannot have intersected the box at all, the check flags with the configured actions, and the Hitboxes check is invoked by Reach to describe the failure.

The reconstruction matters because Grim compensates for client-server position lag: PacketEntityReplication tracks spawned entities, their relative moves and teleports, and ReachInterpolationData keeps the possible box positions across ticks, so the hit is judged against every position the entity could have occupied. Movement allowance is added only when the last movement packet included a position, and the block-impossible-hits setting cancels attacks that no possible look direction could have landed.

The Memeware aura attacks through walls with no line-of-sight check and at ranges up to 8 blocks. For any such hit the reconstructed intercept either misses the box entirely or sits beyond the reach limit, and because the module aims at a fixed eye height while Grim measures from the true eye position, head-level aim against a moving target frequently fails the intersection test. The bot list on the client has no counterpart here: Grim validates whatever C02 arrives against its own entity replication, so filtering targets locally does not reduce the per-hit validation.
